content: The appropriate management of patients should be determined based on the gestational age of the pregnancy. However, it is important to note that oligohydramnios may not become apparent until after the fetus has already sustained irreversible damage. Infants with a history of in utero exposure to Vaseretic should be closely monitored for hypotension, oliguria, and hyperkalemia. Studies in pregnant rats and rabbits have shown no teratogenic effects of enalapril. The doses used in these studies were 57 times and 12 times the maximum recommended human daily dose (MRHDD) on a body surface area basis, respectively. Similarly, no teratogenicity was observed in mice given up to 30 mg/kg/day or in rats given up to 90 mg/kg/day of enalapril in combination with 10 mg/kg/day of hydrochlorothiazide. However, at these doses, fetotoxicity, manifested as a reduction in average fetal weight, was observed in both species. No fetotoxicity occurred at lower doses, such as 30/10 mg/kg/day of enalapril-hydrochlorothiazide in rats and 10/10 mg/kg/day in mice. When ACE inhibitors are used during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, they can cause injury or even death to the developing fetus. If pregnancy is detected, Vaseretic should be discontinued as soon as possible. In cases of oliguria or hypotension, management should focus on supporting blood pressure and renal perfusion. Exchange transfusions or dialysis may be necessary to reverse hypotension and/or compensate for impaired renal function. Enalapril, which crosses the placenta, has been removed from neonatal circulation via peritoneal dialysis with some clinical benefit, and theoretically, it may also be removed by exchange transfusion, although there is no clinical experience with the latter procedure. The safety and effectiveness of this drug in pediatric patients have not been established. Since this drug is substantially excreted by the kidneys, patients with impaired renal function may be at greater risk of toxic reactions. Elderly patients, who are more likely to have reduced renal function, require careful dose selection. Renal function should always be assessed in hypertensive patients, and Vaseretic should be promptly discontinued if necessary, with appropriate therapy and monitoring provided until symptoms resolve completely. Periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts should be considered in patients with collagen vascular disease and renal disease, and renal function should be monitored during the initial weeks of therapy. Single oral doses of enalapril above 1,000 mg/kg in mice and ≥1,775 mg/kg in rats were associated with lethality. The most likely manifestation of overdose is hypotension, which should be treated with intravenous infusion of normal saline. Enalaprilat can be removed from general circulation by hemodialysis and has been removed from neonatal circulation by peritoneal dialysis. Hydrochlorothiazide did not cause lethality after oral doses of 10 g/kg in mice and rats. The most common signs and symptoms of overdose are related to electrolyte depletion (e.g., hypokalemia, hypochloremia, hyponatremia) and dehydration due to excessive diuresis. If digitalis has also been administered, hypokalemia may exacerbate cardiac arrhythmias. Enalapril, after hydrolysis to enalaprilat, inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in humans and animals. ACE is a peptidyl dipeptidase that catalyzes the conversion of angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, which also stimulates aldosterone secretion by the adrenal cortex. Inhibition of ACE results in decreased plasma angiotensin II levels, leading to reduced vasopressor activity and decreased aldosterone secretion. Although the reduction in aldosterone is small, it can cause slight increases in serum potassium levels. In patients treated with enalapril maleate plus a thiazide diuretic, there was essentially no change in serum potassium levels. The removal of angiotensin II's negative feedback on renin secretion leads to increased plasma renin activity. ACE is identical to kininase, an enzyme that degrades bradykinin. Whether increased bradykinin levels, a potent vasodepressor peptide, contribute to the therapeutic effects of enalapril remains unclear. While enalapril's blood pressure-lowering mechanism is believed to primarily involve suppression of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, it is effective even in patients with low-renin hypertension. Although enalapril was antihypertensive in all racial groups studied, Black hypertensive patients (typically a low-renin hypertensive population) had a smaller average response to enalapril monotherapy compared to non-Black patients. In contrast, hydrochlorothiazide was more effective in Black patients than enalapril. However, the concomitant administration of enalapril maleate and hydrochlorothiazide was equally effective in both Black and non-Black patients.
